lesson.title: What "95% Confident" Actually Means (and What It Does Not)
lesson.summary: The confidence level describes the long-run success rate of the interval-building method across repeated samples, not the probability that one already-computed interval contains the fixed true parameter.
lesson.body:
This is the single most commonly misunderstood idea in introductory statistics, so it is worth slowing down for. Once a confidence interval has been calculated from an actual sample, such as the transit survey's 95% interval of 20.75% to 29.25%, it is tempting to say there is a 95% probability that the true proportion is in this interval. That statement is wrong, and understanding exactly why is more important than memorizing the correct wording.

The population parameter, the true proportion p of all adults in the city who support the measure, is a fixed number. It does not change from sample to sample, it simply is whatever it is, even though we do not know its value. Once a specific interval like 20.75% to 29.25% has been calculated from one specific sample, that interval is also fixed: either the true p is inside it, or it is not. There is no more randomness left to assign a probability to. Saying there is a 95% probability p is in this interval treats a fixed, already determined fact as if it were still up for chance, which misunderstands what was actually randomized in this whole process.

What was actually random is the sample itself, and by extension, the method used to build the interval from that sample. The correct interpretation refers to that method's long run behavior: if you were to repeat the entire sampling process many times, drawing a new random sample of the same size each time and building a new confidence interval the same way every time, approximately 95% of all those intervals would contain the true parameter, and about 5% would miss it, purely due to sampling variability. The 95% describes the reliability of the procedure across repeated use, not a probability statement about any single interval that has already been computed.

The statistically correct way to state a conclusion is: "We are 95% confident that the interval from 20.75% to 29.25% captures the true population proportion of adults who support the transit measure." The word "confident" is doing careful work here: it is a statement about trust in the method that produced this interval, backed by the knowledge that the method succeeds 95% of the time in the long run, not a probability statement about this particular interval. Other common misstatements to avoid include "95% of adults support the measure," which wrongly confuses the interval with the data itself, and "95% of sample proportions will fall between 20.75% and 29.25%," which wrongly confuses the confidence interval with the sampling distribution of p-hat, a different, wider spread of typical sample results, not a claim about this specific interval.

This interpretation connects directly to the definition of confidence level from the last chapter. The confidence level is exactly this long run capture rate: the percentage of intervals, built this same way across repeated sampling, that would succeed in containing the true parameter. Keeping that repeated sampling framing in mind is the surest way to avoid the classic misinterpretation and to explain confidence intervals accurately to anyone else.
